chapter: Ch 7: Accounting Standards Based on Items Impacting Financial Statements
unit: Unit 1: AS 4 Contingencies and Events after the Balance Sheet Date
note: AI-written summary of ICAI study material. Check the original for exact wording.

topics.title: Introduction and Scope of AS 4
explain: AS 4 governs accounting treatment for contingencies and events occurring after the balance sheet date.
Most general contingencies are now dealt with under AS 29 rather than AS 4.
AS 4 specifically applies to the impairment of financial assets like provisions for bad and doubtful debts.
A contingency is an existing condition whose ultimate gain or loss depends on uncertain future events.

flow.title: Checking Scope of AS 4 for Contingencies
steps: Identify uncertain condition at reporting date
Check if covered by specific Accounting Standard
If covered by AS 29, apply AS 29
If impairment of receivables, apply AS 4

topics.example: A company evaluates whether to make a provision for doubtful debts at year-end under AS 4.
remember: AS 4 applies to contingencies only to the extent they are not covered by other specific accounting standards.
mistakes: Assuming all contingencies are governed by AS 4 when most general provisions and contingent liabilities fall under AS 29.

quiz.q: Which type of contingency is governed by AS 4 (Revised)?
o: Impairment of receivables like bad debts
quiz.why: AS 4 covers contingencies not governed by other standards, specifically impairment of receivables.

quiz.q: A contingency is an existing situation whose final outcome depends on:
o: One or more uncertain future events
quiz.why: A contingency's outcome is known only when uncertain future events occur or fail to occur.

topics.title: Accounting Treatment of Contingent Losses and Gains
explain: A contingent loss is provided for if it is likely that the contingency will result in a loss.
Management estimates the contingent loss using available evidence, past experience, and expert reports.
If evidence is insufficient or conflicting, disclose the existence and nature of the contingency instead of providing for it.
Guarantees and discounted bills of exchange are generally disclosed in notes even if the loss risk is remote.
Contingent gains are never recognized in financial statements due to prudence, unless realization is virtually certain.

flow.title: Decision Process for Contingent Gains and Losses
steps: Assess outcome of uncertain future event
If contingent gain, do not recognize revenue
If contingent loss is likely, create provision
If loss amount unquantifiable, disclose in notes
If loss possibility is remote, disclose guarantees

topics.example: ABC Ltd sues a debtor for ₹25 Lakhs. Legal team says recovery is nil, so ABC creates a provision for doubtful debts.
remember: Never recognize contingent gains unless realization is virtually certain!
mistakes: Recognizing a contingent gain in the profit and loss account before its realization becomes virtually certain.

quiz.q: How should a contingent gain be treated when its realization is NOT virtually certain?
o: Do not recognize in financial statements
Create an asset in the balance sheet
quiz.why: Contingent gains are not recognized to prevent recognizing revenue that may never be realized.

quiz.q: If it is likely that a contingency will result in a loss to the entity, the entity should:
o: Create a provision in financial statements
Wait until cash is actually paid
Disclose it only in the Directors' Report
quiz.why: Prudence requires providing for expected likely contingent losses.

topics.title: Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date
explain: Post-balance sheet events are significant favorable or unfavorable events occurring between the balance sheet date and the financial statement approval date.
For companies, the approving authority is the Board of Directors.
Events occurring after the approval date are outside the scope of AS 4.
Post-balance sheet events are classified into adjusting events and non-adjusting events.

flow.title: Identifying Relevant Period for Post Balance Sheet Events
steps: Identify Balance Sheet Date
Identify Board approval date for financial statements
Check if event occurred between these dates
If yes, evaluate under AS 4 rules
If after approval date, outside AS 4

topics.example: Financial statements for the year ended 31st March 20X1 are approved on 4th September 20X1. Events from 1st April to 4th September are post-balance sheet events.
remember: The time window for AS 4 ends on the date the financial statements are approved by the approving authority.
mistakes: Including events that occurred after the financial statements were approved by the Board of Directors.

quiz.q: The time period for events occurring after the balance sheet date under AS 4 ends on the date when:
o: The Annual General Meeting is held
Financial statements are approved by Board
quiz.why: AS 4 defines the period up to the date of approval of financial statements by the Board or corresponding authority.

quiz.q: A company with year ended 30.6.20X1 gets board approval on 20.8.20X1. An extra cost event happens on 1.9.20X1. Is this covered by AS 4?
o: No, it occurred after approval date
Yes, disclose in notes to accounts
quiz.why: Events happening after the date of board approval do not fall within the scope of AS 4.

topics.title: Adjusting vs Non-Adjusting Events
explain: Adjusting events provide additional evidence of conditions that already existed at the balance sheet date.
Assets and liabilities must be adjusted in the financial statements for adjusting events.
Non-adjusting events reflect conditions that arose strictly after the balance sheet date.
Non-adjusting events do not result in adjustments to figures in the financial statements.
Significant non-adjusting events are disclosed in the report of the approving authority (Directors' Report).

flow.title: Classifying and Accounting for Post Balance Sheet Events
steps: Detect significant event after Balance Sheet date
Check if condition existed at Balance Sheet date
If condition existed, classify as Adjusting Event
Adjust assets and liabilities in financial statements
If condition arose post reporting date, classify Non-Adjusting
Disclose material non-adjusting events in Board Report

topics.example: A debtor becomes insolvent in April due to heavy loss from a fire in February. Since the fire happened before 31st March, this is an adjusting event.
remember: Existing condition at BS date = Adjusting Event. New condition post BS date = Non-adjusting Event.
mistakes: Adjusting financial statement numbers for a fire that occurred after the balance sheet date when the going concern is unaffected.

quiz.q: A debtor becomes bankrupt in April due to an earthquake that occurred in February (before 31st March). This event is:
quiz.why: The underlying condition (earthquake damage) existed before the balance sheet date, making the bankruptcy an adjusting event.

quiz.q: A major plant is destroyed by fire in May, after the 31st March balance sheet date. Assuming going concern remains valid, how is this handled?
o: Disclosed in the report of approving authority
quiz.why: It is a non-adjusting event because the condition arose after the balance sheet date, requiring disclosure in the Directors' Report.

topics.title: Special Cases: Proposed Dividends and Going Concern
explain: Dividends declared after the balance sheet date but before approval are NOT recognized as liabilities at the balance sheet date.
Such proposed dividends must be disclosed in the notes to accounts as per statutory rules.
If post-balance sheet events show that the entity is no longer a going concern, financial statements cannot be prepared on a going concern basis.
When the going concern assumption becomes invalid, financial statements are prepared on a liquidation basis.

flow.title: Evaluating Going Concern and Proposed Dividend Rules
steps: Identify event occurring after Balance Sheet date
Evaluate impact on Going Concern assumption
If invalid, prepare accounts on Liquidation Basis
If dividend declared after Balance Sheet date
Do not recognize liability at reporting date
Disclose proposed dividend in Notes to Accounts

topics.example: Proposed dividends for the year ended 31st March 2017 declared in May are shown in notes to accounts, not as balance sheet liabilities.
remember: Dividends declared after the balance sheet date require Note disclosure only; no liability is created.
mistakes: Creating a provision or liability in the balance sheet for proposed dividends declared after the balance sheet date.

quiz.q: How are dividends declared after the balance sheet date but before approval treated in financial statements?
o: Recognized as a liability on the balance sheet date
Disclosed only in the notes to accounts
quiz.why: No legal obligation exists on the balance sheet date, so proposed dividends are disclosed only in notes to accounts.

quiz.q: If events after the balance sheet date indicate that the enterprise is no longer a going concern, the financial statements must be prepared on:
quiz.why: If the going concern assumption is no longer valid, financial statements must be prepared on a liquidation basis.

topics.title: Disclosure Requirements and Practical Case Applications
explain: Required disclosures for post-balance sheet events include the nature of the event and an estimate of its financial effect (or a statement that an estimate cannot be made).
Cheques dated 31st March or earlier but received after 31st March are non-adjusting events because the entity lacked custody/control on 31st March.
Frauds occurring during the financial year but detected after the balance sheet date (before approval) are adjusting events.
Court orders delivered before financial statement approval regarding pre-existing legal suits are adjusting events requiring upward or downward adjustments.

flow.title: Handling Post Balance Sheet Court Decrees and Frauds
steps: Identify fraud or lawsuit relating to reporting year
Notice court decree or detection before approval
Classify event as an Adjusting Event
Adjust figures in financial statements accordingly
Disclose nature and estimated financial effect

topics.example: Raj Ltd is sued during 20X1-X2 and provisions ₹10 lakhs. On 18th May (before Board approval on 30th May), the court awards ₹14 lakhs. Raj Ltd adjusts provision upward by ₹4 lakhs.
remember: Events that provide additional evidence of conditions existing on the balance sheet date require adjusting the financial figures.
mistakes: Recognizing cheques received in April (dated March) as cash in hand on 31st March, even though the company had no control over them on 31st March.

quiz.q: Theft of ₹5 lakhs by a cashier in January 20X1 was detected in May 20X1 before approval of accounts for the year ended 31st March 20X1. The loss should be:
o: Ignored as it was detected in May
Adjusted in accounts for year ended 31st March 20X1
Recorded in next year as a prior period item
quiz.why: The theft took place during the accounting period, so its detection before board approval is an adjusting event.

quiz.q: Cheques dated 31st March received by a company in April before board approval should be treated on 31st March as:
o: Not recognized as an asset on 31st March
quiz.why: The entity did not have control or custody of the cheques on 31st March, so they cannot be recognized as an asset on 31st March.
